reminder: An exponential Diophantine equation asks for integer solutions where the unknowns also appear in exponents.
definition: An exponential Diophantine equation is a [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) in which some of the unknowns also occur in [exponents](c:power), as in $3^x-2^y=1$. A solution is a tuple of [integers](c:integer) that satisfies the equation.
examples: The equation $3^x-2^y=1$ has exactly the positive solutions $(x,y)=(1,1)$ and $(2,3)$.
The Ramanujan-Nagell equation $x^2+7=2^n$ has the unknown $n$ in an exponent, and its solutions have $n=3,4,5,7,15$.
Non-example: $x^2+y^2=z^2$ is a Diophantine equation but not an exponential one, because every exponent is a fixed number.

steps: Take a [Diophantine equation](c:diophantine-equation) $P(x_1,\dots,x_n)=0$, where $P$ is a polynomial with integer coefficients.
In $P$, every exponent is a fixed natural number, such as the $2$ in $x^2$.
A fixed exponent is a special case of an exponent that may contain unknowns, so $P=0$ is also an exponential Diophantine equation.
The general concept adds the freedom to put unknowns in exponents, and then the equation is no longer a polynomial equation.
links.why: Every polynomial Diophantine equation is an exponential one, but unknown exponents call for different methods.

reminder: An exponential sum is a finite sum of terms $e^{2\pi i f(n)}$ with real phases $f(n)$.
definition: An exponential sum is a sum $\sum_{n\in S}e(f(n))$ over a finite set $S$, where $e(t)=e^{2\pi i t}$ is the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) of an imaginary number and $f$ is a real function on $S$. Each term is a [complex number](c:complex-number) of absolute value $1$, so the sum has absolute value at most $|S|$, and the aim is to show cancellation below this bound.
examples: A quadratic Gauss sum $\sum_{n=0}^{p-1}e(an^2/p)$ for an odd prime $p$ with $p\nmid a$ has absolute value $\sqrt p$.
A Weyl sum $\sum_{n=1}^{N}e(\alpha n^k)$ for a real number $\alpha$ and an integer $k\ge1$.
The geometric sum $\sum_{n=1}^{N}e(n\alpha)$ has absolute value at most $1/(2\|\alpha\|)$ when $\alpha$ is not an integer, where $\|\alpha\|$ is the distance to the nearest integer.
Non-example: $\sum_{n=1}^{N}e^{-n}$ is not an exponential sum, because $e^{-n}$ is real with absolute value below $1$, not a unit phase.

reminder: A relation is extensional when two elements with the same predecessors are equal.
definition: A [relation](c:relation) $\prec$ on a [set](c:set) $X$ is extensional when, for all $x,y\in X$, the equality $\{z\in X:z\prec x\}=\{z\in X:z\prec y\}$ implies $x=y$. So each [element](c:element) is determined by the elements that lie below it.
examples: The order $<$ on $\mathbb N$ is extensional, because the predecessors of $n$ are $0,\dots,n-1$ and these sets are different for different $n$.
Membership $\in$ on a transitive set is extensional, because the predecessors of $x$ are exactly the elements of $x$, so the [axiom of extensionality](c:axiom-of-extensionality) applies.
Non-example: the empty relation on a set with two elements is not extensional, because both elements have no predecessors but they are different.

steps: Let $<$ be a [well-order](c:is-well-order) on $X$, so $<$ is a strict total order with no infinite descending chain.
Take $x\ne y$ in $X$; by totality, say $x<y$.
Then $x$ is a predecessor of $y$, but $x$ is not a predecessor of $x$, because $<$ is irreflexive.
So $x$ and $y$ have different predecessor sets, and only totality and irreflexivity were used.
links.why: Every well-order is extensional, and extensionality alone is the part that lets one identify elements by their predecessors.

reminder: An extensive-form game describes a game as a tree of moves, with players, information sets and payoffs at the leaves.
definition: An extensive-form game is given by a finite [rooted tree](c:rooted-tree) of positions. Each node that is not a leaf belongs to one player or to chance, its outgoing edges are the actions there, and a chance node carries a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on its actions. The nodes of each player are partitioned into information sets of nodes that the player cannot tell apart, and each leaf carries a payoff for every player.
examples: Tic-tac-toe: the nodes are boards, the players move in turn, the leaves are win, loss or draw, and every information set is a single node.
Poker: a chance node deals the cards, and an information set of one player holds the positions that differ only in the hidden cards of the others.
Non-example: a bare payoff matrix, as for rock-paper-scissors, is a normal-form game, because it has no tree of moves and no information sets.

reminder: A face of a cell complex is one of its two-dimensional cells, a disk bounded by a closed chain of edges.
definition: A face of a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) is a cell of dimension $2$, a disk whose boundary is attached along a closed chain of edges. The faces of a [polyhedron](c:polyhedron) are its flat polygons, and the faces of a [plane graph](c:plane-graph) are the connected regions into which the drawing cuts the plane.
examples: A cube has $6$ faces, and each face is a square.
The drawing of a triangle in the plane has $2$ faces, the inside and the unbounded outside.
A connected plane graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges has $F=E-V+2$ faces, counting the unbounded one.
Non-example: an edge of a cube is not a face in this sense, because it is a $1$-cell and not a $2$-cell.

reminder: Factorization homology gives a homology theory for framed $n$-manifolds with coefficients in an $E_n$-algebra.
definition: Let $M$ be a [framed manifold](c:framed-manifold) of dimension $n$ and $A$ an [E_n-algebra](c:e-n-algebra) in a [symmetric monoidal](c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-1-category) $(\infty,1)$-category with suitable colimits. The factorization homology $\int_MA$ is the colimit of $A$ over all framed embeddings of finite [disjoint unions](c:disjoint-union) of copies of $\mathbb R^n$ into $M$. It satisfies $\int_{\mathbb R^n}A\simeq A$ and $\int_{M\sqcup N}A\simeq\int_MA\otimes\int_NA$.
examples: For $n=1$, $A$ an associative algebra and $M=S^1$, the factorization homology $\int_{S^1}A$ is the Hochschild homology of $A$.
For a commutative algebra $A$, the factorization homology $\int_MA$ is the tensor $M\otimes A$ of $A$ with the space $M$, also called higher Hochschild homology.
Non-example: a chain complex $V$ with no $E_n$-structure has no factorization homology, because there is no way to multiply the values on disjoint disks inside a larger disk.

steps: Take an $E_1$-algebra $A$, that is an associative algebra, and the circle $S^1$ with its framing.
The disks embedded in $S^1$ are intervals, and the colimit over them glues copies of $A$ around the circle.
This gluing gives the derived tensor product $A\otimes^{L}_{A\otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}}A$, which is the [Hochschild homology](c:hochschild-homology) of $A$.
links.why: Hochschild homology is factorization homology on the circle, and higher dimensions give the same construction on other manifolds.

reminder: A family of subsets of $S$ is a function that assigns a subset of $S$ to each index.
definition: A [family](c:family) of subsets of a [set](c:set) $S$ is an index set $I$ with a [function](c:function) $i\mapsto A_i$ from $I$ to the [power set](c:power-set) of $S$, written $(A_i)_{i\in I}$. Two indices may give the same subset, so a family is more than the set of its members.
examples: The intervals $A_n=(0,1/n)$ for $n\ge1$ form a family of subsets of $\mathbb R$ indexed by the positive integers.
The singletons $\{s\}$ for $s\in S$ form a family of subsets of $S$ indexed by $S$.
For $I=\{1,2\}$ and $A_1=A_2=\{0\}$, the family has two indices but only one different subset.
Non-example: a function $f:I\to S$ is not a family of subsets, because it assigns an element and not a subset to each index.

steps: A [family](c:family) in a collection $X$ is a function $i\mapsto x_i$ from an index set $I$ into $X$.
Take for $X$ the power set of $S$, so that each $x_i$ is a subset of $S$.
Then the family is exactly a family of subsets of $S$.
The special case adds that every member is a subset of one fixed set $S$.
links.why: Because all members lie in one set $S$, the union and the intersection of the family make sense.

reminder: A Fermat number is an integer of the form $2^{2^k}+1$ with $k\ge0$.
definition: The $k$-th Fermat number is $F_k=2^{2^k}+1$ for each [integer](c:integer) $k\ge0$, so it is a [power](c:power) of $2$ plus $1$ with an exponent that is itself a power of $2$. A [prime number](c:prime-number) of this form is a Fermat prime.
examples: The first Fermat numbers are $F_0=3$, $F_1=5$, $F_2=17$, $F_3=257$ and $F_4=65537$, and all five are prime.
The number $F_5=2^{32}+1=641\cdot6700417$ is a Fermat number that is not prime.
Non-example: $9=2^3+1$ is not a Fermat number, because the exponent $3$ is not a power of $2$.

steps: Take a [Fermat prime](c:fermat-prime) $p$.
By definition $p$ is prime and $p=2^{2^k}+1$ for some $k\ge0$.
So $p=F_k$ is a Fermat number, and the special case adds only that $F_k$ is prime.
links.why: Statements about all Fermat numbers cover the Fermat primes, and one can ask which Fermat numbers are prime.

reminder: The fiber of $f:E\to B$ over $b$ is the set of points of $E$ that $f$ maps to $b$.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f:E\to B$ and a [point](c:point) $b\in B$, the fiber over $b$ is the [preimage](c:preimage) $f^{-1}(b)=\{e\in E:f(e)=b\}$. For a [bundle](c:bundle) $E\to B$, the fibers over the points of $B$ are the pieces that the bundle glues together.
examples: For the projection $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$, $(x,y)\mapsto x$, the fiber over $a$ is the vertical line $\{a\}\times\mathbb R$.
For the Hopf map $S^3\to S^2$, every fiber is a circle.
For a group homomorphism $\varphi:G\to H$, the fiber over the identity is the kernel of $\varphi$, and each other nonempty fiber is a coset of the kernel.
Non-example: the preimage $f^{-1}(\{b,b'\})$ of two points is not a fiber, because it is the union of two fibers.

steps: The [preimage](c:preimage) of a subset $S\subseteq B$ under $f:E\to B$ is $f^{-1}(S)=\{e\in E:f(e)\in S\}$.
Take for $S$ the one-point subset $\{b\}$.
Then $f^{-1}(\{b\})=\{e\in E:f(e)=b\}$, which is the fiber over $b$.
links.why: A fiber is the preimage of one point, so facts about preimages hold for fibers, and the fibers cut $E$ into disjoint pieces.

steps: Take a map $f:E\to B$ and a point $b$ of $B$, seen as a map $b:1\to B$ from a one-point set.
The [pullback](c:pullback) of $f$ along $b$ is the set of pairs $(e,*)$ with $f(e)=b(*)$.
This set is in bijection with $\{e\in E:f(e)=b\}$, so it is the fiber.
So the fiber is the pullback along a point, and this defines fibers in any category with pullbacks and a terminal object.
links.why: In a general category the fiber is defined as this pullback, so the word carries over from sets.

reminder: A fibration over the circle is a bundle $M\to S^1$, so $M$ is a mapping torus of a self-homeomorphism of the fiber.
definition: A manifold $M$ fibers over the [circle](c:circle) when there is a locally trivial [bundle](c:bundle) $p:M\to S^1$ whose fiber $F$ is a manifold, and $p$ is the fibration. Then $M$ is the mapping torus $F\times[0,1]/(x,1)\sim(\varphi(x),0)$ of a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) $\varphi:F\to F$, and for a [3-manifold](c:3-manifold) the fiber $F$ is a surface.
examples: The torus $T^2=S^1\times S^1$ fibers over $S^1$ by the first projection, with fiber $S^1$.
The complement of the figure-eight knot in $S^3$ fibers over $S^1$, with a once-punctured torus as fiber.
Non-example: the sphere $S^3$ does not fiber over $S^1$, because a bundle over $S^1$ with connected fiber has a fundamental group that maps onto $\mathbb Z$, while $S^3$ is simply connected.

steps: Take a [bundle](c:bundle) $p:E\to B$ with fiber $F$.
Choose the base $B$ to be the circle $S^1$.
Then $p$ is a fibration over the circle, and cutting $S^1$ at one point shows that $E$ is a mapping torus of $F$.
The special case adds that the base is a circle, which gives one monodromy homeomorphism of $F$.
links.why: A fibration over the circle is described by one surface and one homeomorphism, the monodromy.

reminder: A fibred category is a functor $p:E\to B$ where every morphism of $B$ has a Cartesian lift to each object over its target.
definition: A fibred category over a [category](c:category) $B$ is a [functor](c:functor) $p:E\to B$ such that for every morphism $f:b'\to b$ in $B$ and every object $e$ of $E$ with $p(e)=b$ there is a [Cartesian morphism](c:cartesian-morphism) $\varphi:e'\to e$ with $p(\varphi)=f$. This Cartesian lift of $f$ is unique up to a unique isomorphism over $b'$.
examples: The codomain functor $\mathrm{Arr}(B)\to B$ on the arrow category of a category $B$ with pullbacks is a fibred category, and its Cartesian lifts are pullbacks.
The projection $B\times C\to B$ is a fibred category, and the lift of $f$ at $(b,c)$ is $(f,\mathrm{id}_c)$.
A functor $B^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Cat}$ gives a fibred category over $B$ by the [Grothendieck construction](c:grothendieck-construction).
Non-example: the inclusion of the discrete category on two objects into the category $0\to1$ is not fibred, because the morphism $0\to1$ has no lift at the object $1$.

steps: A [discrete fibration](c:discrete-fibration) is a functor $p:E\to B$ such that each morphism of $B$ has exactly one lift at each object over its target.
Uniqueness of lifts makes every lift Cartesian, because a lift of a composite factors uniquely through the lift of its first factor.
So $p$ is a fibred category.
The general case drops uniqueness, and a Cartesian lift is then unique only up to unique isomorphism.
links.why: Discrete fibrations are the fibred categories whose fibers are sets, and the general case has categories as fibers.

reminder: A finite automaton has finitely many states, reads a word letter by letter, and accepts when it stops in an accepting state.
definition: A deterministic finite automaton is a tuple $(Q,\Sigma,\delta,q_0,F)$ with a [finite set](c:finite-set) $Q$ of states, a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, a transition [function](c:function) $\delta:Q\times\Sigma\to Q$, a start state $q_0\in Q$ and a set $F\subseteq Q$ of accepting states. It accepts a word $a_1\cdots a_n$ when the states $q_i=\delta(q_{i-1},a_i)$ that start at $q_0$ end with $q_n\in F$, and the set of accepted words is a [regular language](c:regular-language).
examples: Two states that swap on the letter $1$ and stay on the letter $0$, with the first state accepting, accept exactly the words over $\{0,1\}$ with an even number of $1$s.
Three states that remember how much of $ab$ was just read accept the words over $\{a,b\}$ that end in $ab$.
Non-example: no finite automaton accepts $\{a^nb^n:n\ge0\}$, because the machine would have to count $n$ with finitely many states.

steps: An [automaton](c:automaton) has states, a start state and rules that move it between states when it reads input symbols.
Require that the set of states is finite and that each state and symbol give exactly one next state.
Add a set of accepting states to decide which words the machine accepts.
The result is a finite automaton, and the condition that the special case adds is that the number of states is finite.
links.why: Finiteness of the state set is the whole restriction, and it limits the accepted languages to regular ones.

reminder: A family of sets has finite character when a set belongs to it exactly when all its finite subsets do.
definition: A [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) $\mathcal F$ has finite character when, for every set $A$, we have $A\in\mathcal F$ exactly when every [finite](c:finite-set) [subset](c:subset) of $A$ belongs to $\mathcal F$. Such a family is closed under subsets and under unions of chains.
examples: The linearly independent subsets of a [vector space](c:vector-space) have finite character, because a dependence relation uses only finitely many vectors.
The chains of a partially ordered set have finite character, because a set is a chain exactly when each two of its elements are comparable.
Non-example: the bounded subsets of $\mathbb R$ do not have finite character, because $\mathbb N$ is not bounded although all its finite subsets are bounded.

reminder: A finite cover of a space $X$ is a cover of $X$ by finitely many sets.
definition: A [covering](c:covering) of a set or space $X$ is a [family of subsets](c:family-of-subsets) whose union is $X$. A finite cover is a covering whose index set is a [finite set](c:finite-set), so it has only finitely many members.
examples: The circle $S^1$ has a finite cover by two open arcs, each of which misses one point.
The interval $[0,1]$ has a finite cover by the two closed intervals $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $[\tfrac12,1]$.
Non-example: the open sets $(1/n,1]$ for $n\ge2$ cover $(0,1]$, but there are infinitely many of them, so this is not a finite cover.
Non-example: the two sets $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $[\tfrac34,1]$ are finitely many, but they do not cover $[0,1]$.

steps: A [covering](c:covering) of $X$ is a family $(U_i)_{i\in I}$ of subsets whose union is $X$.
Take a covering whose index set $I$ is finite.
This is a finite cover.
The special case adds only that $I$ is finite.
links.why: Compactness asks that every open cover has a finite subcover, so finite covers are the target of that definition.

reminder: A finite CW complex is a CW complex built from finitely many cells.
definition: A finite CW complex is a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) with only finitely many cells. Equivalently, it is built from the empty space by finitely many [cell attachments](c:attach-cells) of disks $D^k$ along maps from their boundary spheres.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ has a CW structure with one $0$-cell and one $n$-cell.
The torus has a CW structure with one $0$-cell, two $1$-cells and one $2$-cell.
Every finite simplicial complex is a finite CW complex, with one cell for each simplex.
Non-example: the infinite sphere $S^\infty$ has cells in every dimension, so it is a CW complex but not a finite one.

steps: A [CW complex](c:cw-complex) is built by attaching cells dimension by dimension.
Suppose that only finitely many cells are attached in total.
Then the complex is compact, because it is a finite union of images of closed disks.
The special case adds the finiteness of the set of cells.
links.why: A finite CW complex is compact and has a finite description, so counting its cells gives invariants such as the Euler characteristic.

reminder: A finite-dimensional Hilbert space is an inner product space of finite dimension, and completeness holds automatically.
definition: A finite-dimensional Hilbert space is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) whose underlying [vector space](c:vector-space) is a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space). Every finite-dimensional [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) is complete, so the two notions agree. An orthonormal basis identifies it with $\mathbb C^n$ and the inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i\overline{x_i}y_i$.
examples: The space $\mathbb C^n$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_i\overline{x_i}y_i$.
The space $M_n(\mathbb C)$ of matrices with $\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$ has dimension $n^2$.
The state space of a qubit is the Hilbert space $\mathbb C^2$.
Non-example: $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ is a Hilbert space but has infinite dimension.

steps: A [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is an inner product space that is complete in its norm.
Assume that a basis of $H$ as a vector space is finite.
Then $H$ is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and every orthonormal basis has the same finite size.
The special case adds finite dimension, which makes completeness automatic and every linear map bounded.
links.why: Finite dimension removes the analysis, so every theorem on Hilbert spaces holds, and linear algebra gives more.

reminder: A finite flat group scheme over $S$ is a group scheme whose structure map is finite and flat.
definition: A finite flat group scheme over a base scheme $S$ is a [group scheme](c:group-scheme) $G\to S$ whose structure morphism is finite and [flat](c:flat-morphism). Over a Noetherian base $S$, this means that $\mathcal O_G$ is a [locally free](c:locally-free-module) $\mathcal O_S$-module of finite rank, and its rank, which is locally constant on $S$, is the order of $G$.
examples: The constant group scheme $\mathbb Z/n$ over $\operatorname{Spec}R$, with coordinate ring $R^n$.
The group scheme $\mu_n=\operatorname{Spec}R[x]/(x^n-1)$ of $n$-th roots of unity, which has order $n$.
The group scheme $\alpha_p=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb F_p[x]/(x^p)$ in characteristic $p$, which has order $p$.
Non-example: the multiplicative group $\mathbb G_m=\operatorname{Spec}R[x,x^{-1}]$ is flat over $R$ but not finite.

steps: A [group scheme](c:group-scheme) $G\to S$ is a group object in the category of schemes over $S$.
Require that $G\to S$ is finite, so $G$ is affine over $S$ and $\mathcal O_G$ is a finitely generated $\mathcal O_S$-module.
Require also that $G\to S$ is flat, so $\mathcal O_G$ is a flat $\mathcal O_S$-module.
Over a Noetherian base these two conditions give a locally constant order, the rank of $\mathcal O_G$.
links.why: Every result on group schemes applies, and finiteness and flatness add a well-defined order.

reminder: A graph is finite when both its set of vertices and its set of edges are finite.
definition: A finite graph is a [graph](c:graph) whose set of vertices and whose set of edges are both [finite sets](c:finite-set). In a simple finite graph with $|V|$ vertices, the number of edges is at most $\binom{|V|}{2}$.
examples: The complete graph $K_4$ has $4$ vertices and $6$ edges.
The cycle $C_n$ has $n$ vertices and $n$ edges.
Non-example: the graph on $\mathbb Z$ with an edge between $n$ and $n+1$ for every $n$ has infinitely many vertices, so it is not finite.

steps: A [graph](c:graph) has a set $V$ of vertices and a set $E$ of edges, and each edge joins vertices.
Assume that both $V$ and $E$ are finite sets.
The result is a finite graph.
For a simple graph, finiteness of $V$ already implies finiteness of $E$.
links.why: Finite graphs allow counting arguments and induction on the number of vertices.

reminder: A finite subgroup of $SU(2)$ is a finite group of unitary $2\times2$ matrices of determinant $1$.
definition: A finite subgroup of [SU(2)](c:su-2) is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of the group of unitary $2\times2$ complex matrices with determinant $1$ that has finitely many elements. By the classification, each such group is cyclic, binary dihedral, binary tetrahedral, binary octahedral or binary icosahedral.
examples: The cyclic group of order $n$ generated by $\operatorname{diag}(\zeta,\zeta^{-1})$ with $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}$.
The quaternion group $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$, seen as unit quaternions in $SU(2)$.
The binary icosahedral group of order $120$, the preimage of the rotation group of the icosahedron under $SU(2)\to SO(3)$.
Non-example: the alternating group $A_5$ is not a subgroup of $SU(2)$, because $SU(2)$ has only one element of order $2$, namely $-I$, and $A_5$ has fifteen.

steps: A [finite group](c:finite-group) is a group with finitely many elements.
A finite subgroup $G$ of $SU(2)$ has finitely many elements, so it is a finite group under matrix multiplication.
The special case adds an embedding $G\hookrightarrow SU(2)$, which is a faithful unitary representation of dimension $2$ with determinant $1$.
links.why: General facts on finite groups apply, and the embedding gives a $2$-dimensional representation to work with.

steps: The [quaternion group](c:quaternion-group) $Q_8$ is $\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ inside the unit quaternions.
The unit quaternions form a group that is isomorphic to $SU(2)$.
So $Q_8$ is a finite subgroup of $SU(2)$ of order $8$.
The general concept also contains the cyclic groups, the other binary dihedral groups and the three polyhedral groups.
links.why: The quaternion group is the smallest non-cyclic finite subgroup of $SU(2)$.

reminder: A category is finitely complete when every finite diagram in it has a limit.
definition: A [category](c:category) $C$ is finitely complete when it has all [finite limits](c:finite-limit), that is, a limit for every diagram $F:J\to C$ with $J$ a finite category. Equivalently, $C$ has a [terminal object](c:terminal-object) and all [pullbacks](c:pullback).
examples: The categories $\mathrm{Set}$, $\mathrm{Grp}$ and $\mathrm{Top}$ have all limits, so they are finitely complete.
A poset with a greatest element and all binary meets is finitely complete, for example the open sets of a space ordered by inclusion.
Non-example: the discrete category on two objects has no terminal object, because neither object receives a morphism from the other.

steps: A [complete category](c:complete-category) has a limit for every small diagram.
A finite category is a small category, so every finite diagram is a small diagram.
So a complete category has all finite limits and is finitely complete.
The general concept keeps only the finite diagrams, so it also covers the category of finite sets.
links.why: A result that uses only finite limits holds in every complete category, and also in categories such as the finite sets.

steps: An [abelian category](c:abelian-category) has finite products, and every morphism has a kernel.
The equalizer of two morphisms $f$ and $g$ is the kernel of $f-g$.
So it has finite products and equalizers, hence all finite limits.
links.why: Every abelian category is finitely complete, so the finite-limit tools apply to modules and sheaves of modules.

reminder: A group is finitely presented when it has finitely many generators and finitely many defining relations.
definition: A [group](c:group) $G$ is finitely presented when $G\cong F(S)/N$, where $F(S)$ is the [free group](c:free-group) on a finite set $S$ and $N$ is the normal closure of a finite set $R\subseteq F(S)$ of relations. The notation $\langle S\mid R\rangle$ records this [presentation](c:group-presentation).
examples: The group $\mathbb Z^2$ has the presentation $\langle a,b\mid aba^{-1}b^{-1}\rangle$.
Every finite group is finitely presented, for example $S_3=\langle s,t\mid s^2,t^2,(st)^3\rangle$.
The [braid group](c:braid-group) $B_n$ has the generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ and finitely many braid relations.
Non-example: $(\mathbb Q,+)$ is not finitely generated, so it is not finitely presented, and the lamplighter group $\mathbb Z/2\wr\mathbb Z$ is finitely generated but not finitely presented.

steps: A [finitely generated group](c:finitely-generated-group) has a finite generating set $S$, so $G\cong F(S)/N$ for some normal subgroup $N$.
Take $G$ finitely presented, so that $N$ is the normal closure of a finite set of relations.
The finite set $S$ already generates $G$, so $G$ is finitely generated.
The special case adds that $N$ itself needs only finitely many relations.
links.why: A finitely presented group is given by a finite list of generators and relations, which a finitely generated group may lack.

reminder: A morphism of schemes is finitely presented when it is locally of finite presentation, quasi-compact and quasi-separated.
definition: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ is locally of finite presentation when, for all affine opens $\operatorname{Spec}A\subseteq X$ and $\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq Y$ with $f(\operatorname{Spec}A)\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}R$, the $R$-algebra $A$ has [finite presentation](c:finite-presentation), that is, $A\cong R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(g_1,\dots,g_m)$. The morphism $f$ is finitely presented when it is also [quasi-compact](c:quasi-compact) and [quasi-separated](c:quasi-separated).
examples: The projection $\mathbb A^n_Y\to Y$ is finitely presented, because $\mathbb A^n_Y$ is locally $\operatorname{Spec}R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over $\operatorname{Spec}R$.
A closed immersion $\operatorname{Spec}R/I\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ is finitely presented when the ideal $I$ is finitely generated.
Every morphism of finite type between Noetherian schemes is finitely presented.

Non-example: for $R=k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$, the closed immersion $\operatorname{Spec}k\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ given by $x_i\mapsto0$ has finite type but is not finitely presented, because the ideal $(x_1,x_2,\dots)$ is not finitely generated.

steps: A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is of [finite type](c:finite-type) when it is quasi-compact and each local algebra has the form $A\cong R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/I$.
Take $f$ finitely presented, so that $A\cong R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(g_1,\dots,g_m)$.
This has the same form with $I=(g_1,\dots,g_m)$, so $f$ is of finite type.
The special case adds that the ideal $I$ is finitely generated.
links.why: Finite type controls the generators, and finite presentation controls the relations too, which allows limit arguments.

reminder: The first fundamental form of a surface in $\mathbb R^3$ is the Euclidean inner product restricted to each tangent plane.
definition: For a [regular surface](c:regular-surface) $S\subset\mathbb R^3$ and a point $p\in S$, the first fundamental form is the [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $\mathrm I_p(w)=\langle w,w\rangle$ on the [tangent plane](c:tangent-space) $T_pS$. For a parametrization $x(u,v)$ it is $E\,du^2+2F\,du\,dv+G\,dv^2$, with $E=\langle x_u,x_u\rangle$, $F=\langle x_u,x_v\rangle$ and $G=\langle x_v,x_v\rangle$.
examples: For the plane $x(u,v)=(u,v,0)$, we have $E=G=1$ and $F=0$, so $\mathrm I=du^2+dv^2$.
For the unit sphere with $x(\theta,\varphi)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$, we have $\mathrm I=d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$.
For the cylinder $x(u,v)=(\cos u,\sin u,v)$, we have $\mathrm I=du^2+dv^2$, the same as for the plane.
Non-example: the second fundamental form $L\,du^2+2M\,du\,dv+N\,dv^2$ measures how the surface bends in $\mathbb R^3$, and it is not the first fundamental form.

steps: An [induced metric](c:induced-metric) pulls the metric of an ambient space back to a submanifold along the inclusion.
Take $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean inner product and the inclusion of the surface $S$.
At $p$ the induced metric sends $w\in T_pS$ to $\langle w,w\rangle$, which is the first fundamental form.
The special case fixes the ambient space as $\mathbb R^3$ and the submanifold as a surface.
links.why: Lengths, angles and areas on the surface follow from the first fundamental form alone.

reminder: The Fisher information of a parameter is the variance of the score, the derivative of the log-likelihood.
definition: Let a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ have a [probability density](c:probability-density) $f(x;\theta)$ that depends smoothly on a real parameter $\theta$, with a support that does not depend on $\theta$. The Fisher information is $I(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\big[(\partial_\theta\log f(X;\theta))^2\big]$, which is the [variance](c:variance) of the score $\partial_\theta\log f(X;\theta)$, because under mild regularity conditions the score has [expected value](c:expected-value) $0$.
examples: For $X\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2)$ with known $\sigma$, the Fisher information is $I(\theta)=1/\sigma^2$.
For a Bernoulli variable with parameter $p$, the Fisher information is $I(p)=1/(p(1-p))$.
For $n$ independent observations, the Fisher information is $nI(\theta)$.
Non-example: for $X$ uniform on $[0,\theta]$ the support depends on $\theta$ and the score $-1/\theta$ has mean $-1/\theta\ne0$, so the formula does not give the information of the Cramer-Rao bound.

reminder: The fixed point space of a group action is the subspace of points that every group element leaves unchanged.
definition: Let a [group](c:group) $G$ act on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$. The fixed point space is $X^G=\{x\in X:gx=x\text{ for all }g\in G\}$ with the [subspace topology](c:subspace-topology).
examples: For $\mathbb Z/2$ acting on $S^2$ by $(x,y,z)\mapsto(-x,-y,z)$, the fixed point space is the two poles.
For $\mathbb Z/2$ acting on $S^2$ by the reflection $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,-z)$, the fixed point space is the equator.
For the trivial action, the fixed point space is all of $X$.
Non-example: the orbit space $X/G$ is not $X^G$, because it keeps every orbit, while $X^G$ keeps only the points whose orbit has one point.

steps: The fixed-point space $X^H$ of a subgroup $H$ is the set of points that every element of $H$ fixes.
Choose $H=G$, the whole group that acts.
Then $X^H=X^G$, so each fixed point space of an action is a case of the general one.
The general concept also lets $H$ be a smaller subgroup, which gives a family of subspaces $X^H$.
links.why: Equivariant homotopy theory studies all the spaces $X^H$ together, and $X^G$ is the one for the whole group.

reminder: For a $G$-space $X$ and a subgroup $H$, the fixed-point space $X^H$ holds the points that $H$ fixes.
definition: For a [group action](c:group-action) of $G$ on a space $X$ and a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $H\le G$, the fixed-point space is $X^H=\{x\in X:hx=x\text{ for all }h\in H\}$ with the [subspace topology](c:subspace-topology). An [equivariant](c:equivariant) map $f:X\to Y$ restricts to maps $f^H:X^H\to Y^H$, and equivariant theorems compare $f$ with all the maps $f^H$.
examples: For $G=\mathbb Z/2$ acting on $S^n$ by the antipodal map, $X^G=\varnothing$ while $X^{\{e\}}=S^n$.
For $G=S^1$ acting on $S^2$ by rotation about an axis, $X^G$ is the two poles and $X^{\{e\}}=S^2$.
For $\mathbb Z$ acting on $\mathbb R$ by translation, $X^H=\varnothing$ for every nontrivial subgroup $H$.
Non-example: the orbit space $X/H$ is not $X^H$, because $X^H$ is a subspace of $X$ and $X/H$ is a quotient of $X$.

steps: Take the [fixed point space](c:fixed-point-space) $X^G$ of a $G$-space $X$, the points fixed by every element of $G$.
Choose the subgroup $H=G$ in the definition of $X^H$.
The definition then gives $X^G$, so every fixed point space of a whole action is a special case.
The general concept also lets $H$ be a smaller subgroup, which gives a whole family of subspaces of $X$.
links.why: The family of all $X^H$ detects when an equivariant map is an equivalence, which one fixed point space cannot do.

reminder: A functor $F:C\to\mathrm{Set}$ is flat when it is a filtered colimit of representable functors.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F:C\to\mathrm{Set}$ on a small category $C$ is flat when it is a filtered colimit of [representable functors](c:representable-functor). Equivalently, its category of elements is [cofiltered](c:cofiltered-category). When $C$ has all [finite limits](c:finite-limit), $F$ is flat exactly when it preserves finite limits.
examples: Every representable functor $\mathrm{Hom}(c,-)$ is flat, because its category of elements has an initial object.
For a poset $P$ and a filter $\mathcal F$ in $P$, the functor that sends $p$ to a point if $p\in\mathcal F$ and to $\varnothing$ otherwise is flat.
Non-example: the sum $\mathrm{Hom}(a,-)\sqcup\mathrm{Hom}(b,-)$ of two representable functors is not flat, because its category of elements has two separate pieces.

steps: A [representable functor](c:representable-functor) has the form $\mathrm{Hom}(c,-)$ for an object $c$ of $C$.
It is the colimit of itself over the category with one object and one morphism, and this category is filtered.
So it is a filtered colimit of representable functors, hence flat.
The general concept also allows filtered colimits of many representable functors, such as filters in a poset.
links.why: Representable functors are the simplest flat functors, and the flat ones are their filtered colimits.

reminder: A ring homomorphism $R\to S$ is flat when tensoring with $S$ over $R$ keeps exact sequences exact.
definition: A [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) of rings $u:R\to S$ is flat when the functor $M\mapsto S\otimes_RM$ of [extension of scalars](c:extension-of-scalars), from $R$-modules to $S$-modules, is an [exact functor](c:exact-functor). Equivalently, $S$ is a [flat module](c:flat-module) over $R$. A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ is flat when every local map $\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}\to\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is flat.
examples: The inclusion $R\to R[x]$ is flat, because $R[x]$ is a free $R$-module.
A localization $R\to R[s^{-1}]$ is flat, and so is the inclusion $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q$.
Non-example: $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2$ is not flat, because tensoring the injection $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb Z/2$ gives the zero map on $\mathbb Z/2$, which is not injective.

steps: A [flat module](c:flat-module) over $R$ is an $R$-module $M$ such that $M\otimes_R-$ preserves exact sequences.
A ring homomorphism $u:R\to S$ makes $S$ an $R$-module by $r\cdot s=u(r)s$.
The map $u$ is flat exactly when this $R$-module $S$ is flat.
The special case adds the ring structure of $S$, so that $S\otimes_R-$ takes values in $S$-modules.
links.why: Every fact on flat modules applies to a flat ring map, and the ring structure adds base change.

reminder: A flat resolution of a module is a resolution of it by flat modules.
definition: A flat resolution of a [module](c:module) $M$ is an exact sequence $\cdots\to F_2\to F_1\to F_0\to M\to0$ in which every $F_i$ is a [flat module](c:flat-module). For a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $C$, it is a complex $F$ of flat modules with a quasi-isomorphism $F\to C$.
examples: The sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{n}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/n\to0$ is a flat resolution of $\mathbb Z/n$, because $\mathbb Z$ is flat.
Every projective resolution is a flat resolution, because projective modules are flat.
The module $\mathbb Q$ is flat over $\mathbb Z$, so $0\to\mathbb Q\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}\mathbb Q\to0$ is a flat resolution of $\mathbb Q$ of length $0$.
Non-example: $0\to\mathbb Z/2\to\mathbb Z/4\to\mathbb Z/2\to0$ is exact but is not a flat resolution of $\mathbb Z/2$ over $\mathbb Z$, because $\mathbb Z/2$ and $\mathbb Z/4$ are not flat.

steps: A [resolution](c:resolution) of an object $M$ replaces $M$ by an exact sequence of simpler objects $F_i$.
Choose the simpler objects to be flat modules.
The result is a flat resolution.
The special case adds only that each $F_i$ is flat.
links.why: Flat resolutions compute derived tensor products, as free resolutions do, but their terms are more flexible.

steps: A [free resolution](c:free-resolution) of $M$ is a resolution $\cdots\to F_1\to F_0\to M\to0$ in which each $F_i$ is a free module.
Every free module is projective, and every projective module is flat.
So the same sequence is a flat resolution.
The general concept allows flat terms that are not free, such as $\mathbb Q$ over $\mathbb Z$.
links.why: Every free resolution can be used where a flat resolution is needed, and flat ones exist in more cases.

reminder: A forgetful functor sends each object and morphism to its underlying one and drops the extra structure.
definition: A forgetful functor is a [functor](c:functor) $U:C\to D$ that sends an object with extra structure to its underlying object, and a morphism to the same underlying morphism, so it discards structure, properties or stuff. It is usually [faithful](c:faithful), as for $\mathrm{Grp}\to\mathrm{Set}$, which sends a group to its [underlying set](c:underlying-set).
examples: The functor $\mathrm{Grp}\to\mathrm{Set}$ sends a group to its underlying set and a homomorphism to the same function.
The functor $\mathrm{Ab}\to\mathrm{Grp}$ forgets the property of commutativity.
The functor $\mathrm{Top}\to\mathrm{Set}$ forgets the topology.
Non-example: the free group functor $\mathrm{Set}\to\mathrm{Grp}$ adds structure, so it is not forgetful; it is the left adjoint of the forgetful functor.

steps: A [functor](c:functor) sends objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms, and it preserves composition and identities.
Take categories whose objects are sets with extra structure and whose morphisms are maps that preserve it.
Send each object to its underlying set and each morphism to the same map.
This is a functor, because composition and identities of maps do not depend on the structure, and the special case adds that structure is dropped.
links.why: A forgetful functor tells which structure the objects carry, and its adjoints give the free constructions.

reminder: A formal system has a formal language, axioms and inference rules, and its theorems are the formulas derivable from the axioms.
definition: A formal system consists of a [formal language](c:language) with a set of [formulas](c:formula), a set of [axioms](c:axiom) that are formulas, and a set of inference rules that produce a formula from finitely many formulas. A theorem is the last formula of a derivation, which is a finite sequence of formulas in which each one is an axiom or follows from earlier ones by a rule.
examples: Propositional logic with axiom schemes and the single rule modus ponens is a formal system, called a Hilbert system.
Peano arithmetic is a formal system in first-order logic, with axioms for $0$, successor, addition, multiplication and induction.
Hofstadter's MIU system has the axiom $MI$ and four rules that rewrite strings.
Non-example: an informal proof in everyday language is not a derivation in a formal system, because no fixed syntax and no fixed rules decide each step.

reminder: A field is formally real when $-1$ is not a sum of squares in it.
definition: A [field](c:field) $k$ is formally real when $-1$ is not a sum of squares in $k$. Equivalently, $\sum_{i=1}^na_i^2=0$ forces $a_1=\dots=a_n=0$ for every $n$. By the Artin-Schreier theorem, $k$ is formally real exactly when it admits a [total order](c:total-order) that makes it an [ordered field](c:ordered-field).
examples: The fields $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb R$ are formally real, and so is every ordered field, because squares are nonnegative.
The field $\mathbb R(x)$ of rational functions is formally real.
Non-example: $\mathbb C$ is not formally real, because $-1=i^2$.
Non-example: a field of positive characteristic $p$ is not formally real, because $-1=1^2+\dots+1^2$ with $p-1$ terms.

steps: Take an [ordered field](c:ordered-field) $k$, in which squares are nonnegative and sums of nonnegative elements are nonnegative.
Suppose that $\sum a_i^2=0$ and some $a_j\ne0$; then $a_j^2>0$, so the sum is positive, which is a contradiction.
So $-1$ is not a sum of squares, and $k$ is formally real.
The general concept drops the choice of an order, and a formally real field can have many orders.
links.why: A formally real field is a field that can be ordered, with no order chosen yet.

steps: Take a [real closed field](c:is-real-closed) $k$.
By one standard definition, $k$ is formally real and has no proper algebraic extension that is formally real.
So $k$ is formally real.
The general concept drops maximality, and $\mathbb Q$ is formally real but not real closed.
links.why: Real closed fields are the maximal formally real fields, so formally real fields are the ones that sit inside them.

reminder: The forward difference of a function $f$ with step $h$ is $f(x+h)-f(x)$.
definition: The forward difference operator $\Delta_h$ with step $h$ sends a [function](c:function) $f$ to $\Delta_hf(x)=f(x+h)-f(x)$. For a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ and step $1$, it gives $\Delta a_n=a_{n+1}-a_n$, and the iterates satisfy $\Delta^ka_n=\sum_{j=0}^{k}(-1)^{k-j}\binom kj a_{n+j}$.
examples: For $a_n=n^2$, we have $\Delta a_n=2n+1$ and $\Delta^2a_n=2$.
For $a_n=2^n$, we have $\Delta a_n=2^n$.
For a polynomial of degree $d$, the operator $\Delta$ lowers the degree by $1$, so $\Delta^{d+1}$ gives $0$.
Non-example: the backward difference $\nabla f(x)=f(x)-f(x-h)$ uses the earlier point, so it is not the forward difference, although $\nabla f(x)=\Delta f(x-h)$.

reminder: A Fourier integral operator is a linear operator given by an oscillatory integral with a phase function and an amplitude.
definition: A Fourier integral operator is a linear operator $T$ whose [integral kernel](c:integral-kernel) is an oscillatory integral $K(x,y)=\int e^{i\varphi(x,y,\theta)}a(x,y,\theta)\,d\theta$. Here $\varphi$ is a real phase function that is nondegenerate and homogeneous of degree $1$ in $\theta$, and $a$ is a smooth amplitude of symbol type. Then $Tu(x)=\int K(x,y)u(y)\,dy$ in the sense of [distributions](c:distribution).
examples: The half-wave propagator $e^{it\sqrt{-\Delta}}$ is a Fourier integral operator with phase $(x-y)\cdot\theta+t|\theta|$.
Pullback $u\mapsto u\circ\chi$ by a diffeomorphism $\chi$ is a Fourier integral operator with phase $(\chi(x)-y)\cdot\theta$.
Non-example: the squaring map $u\mapsto u^2$ is not linear, so it is not a Fourier integral operator.

steps: A [pseudodifferential operator](c:pseudodifferential-operator) has the form $Pu(x)=(2\pi)^{-n}\iint e^{i(x-y)\cdot\theta}a(x,\theta)u(y)\,dy\,d\theta$ with a symbol $a$.
Take the phase function $\varphi(x,y,\theta)=(x-y)\cdot\theta$, which is real, nondegenerate and homogeneous of degree $1$ in $\theta$.
With the amplitude $a(x,y,\theta)=a(x,\theta)$, the kernel of $P$ has the form required of a Fourier integral operator.
The general concept allows other phase functions, which move singularities instead of keeping them in place.
links.why: Facts on Fourier integral operators apply to pseudodifferential operators, and other phases add operators that move singularities.

reminder: The Fourier-Laplace transform is the Fourier transform with a complex frequency variable $\zeta$.
definition: For a [distribution](c:distribution) $u$ with compact support on $\mathbb R^n$, the Fourier-Laplace transform is $\hat u(\zeta)=\langle u,e^{-i\langle x,\zeta\rangle}\rangle$ for $\zeta\in\mathbb C^n$, and for a function $f$ it is $\int f(x)e^{-i\langle x,\zeta\rangle}\,dx$ where this integral converges. For real $\zeta$ it is the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform), and for $\zeta=-is$ with $s$ real it is the two-sided [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform). By the Paley-Wiener-Schwartz theorem, $\hat u$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function) of exponential type, and the argument $\zeta$ is a [complex number](c:complex-number).
examples: For $u=\delta_a$ on $\mathbb R$, we have $\hat u(\zeta)=e^{-ia\zeta}$.
For $f=\mathbf 1_{[-1,1]}$, we have $\hat f(\zeta)=2\sin\zeta/\zeta$, an entire function of $\zeta$.
For $f(x)=e^{-x}$ on $x>0$ and $0$ elsewhere, we have $\hat f(\zeta)=1/(1+i\zeta)$ for $\operatorname{Im}\zeta<1$, which is defined only in a half-plane.
Non-example: $f(x)=e^{x^2}$ has no Fourier-Laplace transform, because $\int e^{x^2}e^{-ix\zeta}\,dx$ diverges for every $\zeta$.

steps: The [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) of $f$ is $\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-ix\xi}\,dx$ for real $\xi$.
Replace the real number $\xi$ by a complex number $\zeta=\xi+i\eta$.
The integrand becomes $f(x)e^{-ix\zeta}$, and for real $\zeta$ nothing changes.
So the Fourier transform is the restriction of the Fourier-Laplace transform to real $\zeta$.
links.why: Results on the Fourier-Laplace transform give the Fourier transform on the real line, and complex analysis gives more.

steps: The [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) of $f$ is $\int f(x)e^{-sx}\,dx$ for a complex number $s$.
Put $s=i\zeta$, so that $e^{-sx}=e^{-ix\zeta}$.
Then the Laplace transform at $s$ equals the Fourier-Laplace transform at $\zeta=-is$.
So the Laplace transform is the Fourier-Laplace transform along imaginary directions.
links.why: Laplace transforms and Fourier transforms are two views of one transform on the complex plane.

reminder: The free algebra on a set $X$ is the algebra of noncommutative polynomials in the elements of $X$.
definition: Let $k$ be a [field](c:field) and $X$ a [set](c:set). The free algebra $k\langle X\rangle$ is the [algebra](c:algebra) whose basis over $k$ is the [free monoid](c:free-monoid) on $X$, which is the set of all finite words in $X$, and whose product is concatenation of words. It has the universal property that every map $X\to A$ into a $k$-algebra $A$ extends to a unique algebra homomorphism $k\langle X\rangle\to A$.
examples: For $X=\{x\}$, the free algebra $k\langle x\rangle$ is the polynomial ring $k[x]$.
For $X=\{x,y\}$, the words $xy$ and $yx$ are different basis elements, so $xy\ne yx$.
The free algebra on a basis of a vector space $V$ is the tensor algebra of $V$.
Non-example: the polynomial ring $k[x,y]$ is not free on $\{x,y\}$ as an algebra, because $xy=yx$ is a relation.

steps: The [tensor algebra](c:tensor-algebra) of a vector space $V$ is $T(V)=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}V^{\otimes n}$ with the concatenation product.
Take $V$ to be the vector space with basis $X$.
Then $V^{\otimes n}$ has as basis the words of length $n$ in $X$, so $T(V)$ has as basis all words in $X$.
So $T(V)=k\langle X\rangle$, and the special case adds that $V$ comes with a chosen basis.
links.why: A free algebra is the tensor algebra of a vector space with a basis, so facts on tensor algebras apply.

reminder: The free field on a set $X$ is the universal skew field of fractions of the free algebra on $X$.
definition: The free field on a set $X$ over a [field](c:field) $k$ is the universal [division ring](c:division-ring) of fractions $D$ of the [free algebra](c:free-algebra) $k\langle X\rangle$: the algebra embeds in $D$, generates $D$ as a division ring, and every full square matrix over it becomes invertible in $D$. For one generator it is the usual [field of fractions](c:field-of-fractions) $k(x)$. In physics the same words name a different concept, a field with no interaction.
examples: For one generator $x$, the free field is the field $k(x)$ of rational functions.
For two generators $x,y$, the free field contains $x$, $y$, the inverse $(1-xy)^{-1}$, and $xy\ne yx$ in it.
Non-example: the field of rational functions $k(x,y)$ is a field of fractions of $k[x,y]$ but not the free field, because $xy=yx$ there.
Non-example: in physics, a free field is a field whose equation of motion is linear and has no interaction, which is a different concept with the same name.

reminder: A Frobenius element at an unramified prime is the Galois automorphism that acts as $x\mapsto x^q$ on the residue field.
definition: Let $L/K$ be a [Galois extension](c:galois-extension) of [number fields](c:number-field), let $\mathfrak P$ be a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) of $\mathcal O_L$ over a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $\mathcal O_K$ that is [unramified](c:unramified) in $L$, and let $q=|\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak p|$. The Frobenius element $\mathrm{Frob}_{\mathfrak P}$ is the unique element $\sigma$ of the [Galois group](c:galois-group) $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ with $\sigma(x)\equiv x^q\pmod{\mathfrak P}$ for all $x\in\mathcal O_L$. Its conjugacy class depends only on $\mathfrak p$.
examples: For $L=\mathbb Q(i)$, $K=\mathbb Q$ and an odd prime $p$, the Frobenius element is the identity if $p\equiv1\pmod4$ and complex conjugation if $p\equiv3\pmod4$.
For $L=\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)$ and a prime $p\nmid n$, the Frobenius element sends $\zeta_n$ to $\zeta_n^p$.
Non-example: for $L=\mathbb Q(i)$ and $p=2$, which is ramified, no Frobenius element is defined, because both automorphisms satisfy the congruence modulo $(1+i)$, so it does not single out one.

reminder: A functor is full and faithful when it gives a bijection from $C(x,y)$ to $D(Fx,Fy)$ for all objects $x,y$.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $F:C\to D$ is full and faithful when, for all objects $x,y$ of $C$, the function $F:C(x,y)\to D(F(x),F(y))$ on morphisms is a bijection. It is [faithful](c:faithful) when these functions are injective and [full](c:full) when they are surjective.
examples: The inclusion of a full subcategory, such as $\mathrm{Ab}\to\mathrm{Grp}$, is full and faithful.
The Yoneda embedding $C\to[C^{\mathrm{op}},\mathrm{Set}]$ is full and faithful.
Every equivalence of categories is full and faithful.
Non-example: the forgetful functor $\mathrm{Grp}\to\mathrm{Set}$ is faithful but not full, because not every function between groups is a homomorphism.

steps: A [faithful functor](c:faithful) $F$ is injective on each set of morphisms $C(x,y)\to D(Fx,Fy)$.
A full and faithful functor is faithful by definition, because a bijection is injective.
It adds that each such map is also surjective, so every morphism $Fx\to Fy$ comes from a morphism $x\to y$.
links.why: A full and faithful functor reflects morphisms as well as equalities, so $C$ is a copy of its image.

steps: An [equivalence of categories](c:equivalence-of-categories) is a functor $F:C\to D$ with a functor $G:D\to C$ and natural isomorphisms $GF\cong\mathrm{id}$ and $FG\cong\mathrm{id}$.
These isomorphisms make $F$ a bijection from each $C(x,y)$ to $D(Fx,Fy)$.
So $F$ is full and faithful.
The general concept drops essential surjectivity, so it also covers inclusions of full subcategories.
links.why: An equivalence is a full and faithful functor that also hits every object up to isomorphism.

reminder: An object is fully dualizable when it has a dual and the duality maps have adjoints, which have adjoints, up to level $n-1$.
definition: Let $X$ be an object of a [symmetric monoidal $(\infty,n)$-category](c:symmetric-monoidal-infinity-n-category) $\mathcal C$. It is fully dualizable when it is a [dualizable object](c:dualizable-object), with a dual $X^\vee$, an evaluation $X^\vee\otimes X\to1$ and a coevaluation $1\to X\otimes X^\vee$, and these two maps have adjoints, the units and counits of those adjunctions have adjoints, and so on through the morphisms of dimension $n-1$.
examples: In $\mathrm{Vect}_k$ as an $(\infty,1)$-category, fully dualizable means dualizable, which holds exactly for the finite-dimensional vector spaces.
In the framed bordism $(\infty,n)$-category, the point is fully dualizable, and the cobordism hypothesis says that it is the free fully dualizable object.
Non-example: an infinite-dimensional vector space is not dualizable in $\mathrm{Vect}_k$, so it is not fully dualizable.

steps: A [dualizable object](c:dualizable-object) $X$ has a dual $X^\vee$ with evaluation and coevaluation maps that satisfy the zigzag identities.
Take $X$ fully dualizable, so that it has these data.
Then $X$ is dualizable, by forgetting the further adjoints.
The special case adds adjoints for the evaluation and the coevaluation, and then for their units and counits, up to level $n-1$.
links.why: Full dualizability is dualizability at every dimension, and it is the condition that gives a field theory from an object.

reminder: A function assigns to each element of its domain exactly one element of its codomain.
definition: A function $f:A\to B$ between [sets](c:set) is a [relation](c:relation) $f\subseteq A\times B$ such that for each $a\in A$ there is exactly one $b\in B$ with $(a,b)\in f$, and one writes $f(a)=b$. The set $A$ is the domain and the set $B$ is the codomain.
examples: The map $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $f(x)=x^2$.
The identity map $\mathrm{id}_A:A\to A$, and every constant map.
The characteristic function $\mathbf 1_S:A\to\{0,1\}$ of a subset $S\subseteq A$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto\pm\sqrt x$ is not a function $[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$, because $x=4$ has two images, $2$ and $-2$.

steps: A [relation](c:relation) from $A$ to $B$ is a subset $R\subseteq A\times B$.
Take a relation $R$ such that every $a\in A$ is related to at least one $b$.
Require also that every $a\in A$ is related to at most one $b$.
Such a relation is a function, and the special case adds that it is total and single-valued.
links.why: Functions are the relations that one can apply to elements, and composing functions is composing relations.

reminder: A functor sends objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms and preserves composition and identities.
definition: A functor $F:C\to D$ between [categories](c:category) assigns to each object $x$ of $C$ an object $F(x)$ of $D$, and to each morphism $f:x\to y$ a morphism $F(f):F(x)\to F(y)$. It satisfies $F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f)$ and $F(\mathrm{id}_x)=\mathrm{id}_{F(x)}$.
examples: The forgetful functor $\mathrm{Grp}\to\mathrm{Set}$ sends a group to its underlying set.
For an object $A$ of $C$, the functor $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-):C\to\mathrm{Set}$ sends $x$ to the set $C(A,x)$ and $f$ to composition with $f$.
The abelianization $G\mapsto G/[G,G]$ is a functor $\mathrm{Grp}\to\mathrm{Ab}$.

Non-example: the center $G\mapsto Z(G)$ is not a functor on $\mathrm{Grp}$, because the maps $\mathbb Z/2\to S_3\to\mathbb Z/2$ (a transposition, then the sign) compose to the identity, but then the identity of $Z(\mathbb Z/2)=\mathbb Z/2$ would factor through $Z(S_3)=1$.

steps: A [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor) sends a group, ring or space to its underlying set.
It sends each homomorphism to the same underlying function.
Composition and identities of functions are not changed, so it preserves them.
So every forgetful functor is a functor, and the general concept does not need the objects to have structure.
links.why: Forgetful functors are the first examples of functors, and the general definition keeps only composition and identities.

steps: Take an object $A$ of a category $C$.
Define $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ on objects by $x\mapsto C(A,x)$ and on a morphism $f:x\to y$ by $h\mapsto f\circ h$.
Associativity and the identity law of $C$ give $F(g\circ f)=F(g)\circ F(f)$ and $F(\mathrm{id})=\mathrm{id}$.
So $\mathrm{Hom}(A,-)$ is a functor $C\to\mathrm{Set}$, which is a special case of the general concept.
links.why: Representable functors turn the morphisms of $C$ into maps of sets, and the Yoneda lemma describes all their maps.

steps: A group $G$ is a category with one object whose morphisms are the elements of $G$.
A functor between two such categories sends each element to an element and respects composition and identities.
This is exactly a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism).
So group homomorphisms are the functors between one-object categories in which every morphism is invertible.
links.why: The definition of a functor is the definition of a homomorphism with many objects instead of one.

reminder: A fundamental solution of a linear differential operator $P$ is a distribution $E$ with $PE=\delta$.
definition: Let $P$ be a [linear differential operator](c:linear-differential-operator) with constant coefficients on $\mathbb R^n$. A fundamental solution of $P$ is a [distribution](c:distribution) $E$ with $PE=\delta$, where $\delta$ is the [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) at $0$. If $g$ has compact support, the [convolution](c:convolution) $u=E*g$ solves $Pu=g$.
examples: For $P=d/dx$ on $\mathbb R$, the Heaviside function $H$ is a fundamental solution, because $H'=\delta$.
For the Laplacian $\Delta$ on $\mathbb R^3$, the function $E(x)=-1/(4\pi|x|)$ is a fundamental solution.
For the heat operator $\partial_t-\Delta$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, the function $E(t,x)=H(t)(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/(4t)}$ is a fundamental solution.
Non-example: the Heaviside function is not a fundamental solution of $d^2/dx^2$, because $H''=\delta'$ and not $\delta$.

reminder: A Gabor frame is a frame of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ made of time shifts and frequency shifts of one window function.
definition: For a window $g$ in the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $L^2(\mathbb R)$ of [square-integrable functions](c:lp-space) and numbers $a,b>0$, put $g_{m,n}(x)=e^{2\pi ibnx}g(x-am)$ for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$. The family $(g_{m,n})$ is a Gabor frame when there are constants $0<A\le B$ with $A\|f\|^2\le\sum_{m,n}|\langle f,g_{m,n}\rangle|^2\le B\|f\|^2$ for all $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$.
examples: For the Gaussian $g(x)=e^{-\pi x^2}$, the family $(g_{m,n})$ is a Gabor frame when $ab<1$.
For $g=\mathbf 1_{[0,1)}$ and $a=b=1$, the family $(g_{m,n})$ is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(\mathbb R)$, hence a frame.
Non-example: if $ab>1$, no window $g$ gives a frame, because the lattice of shifts is too sparse.
Non-example: the Gaussian with $ab=1$ is not a frame, because by the Balian-Low theorem a frame at this density has a window that is badly localized in time or frequency.

reminder: In a Gale-Stewart game two players alternately choose natural numbers forever, and the infinite sequence decides who wins.
definition: A Gale-Stewart game $G(A)$ is given by a set $A\subseteq\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}$ of infinite [sequences](c:sequence) of [natural numbers](c:natural-number). Players I and II alternately choose natural numbers $x_0,x_1,x_2,\dots$, each seeing all earlier choices, and player I wins when $(x_0,x_1,\dots)\in A$, and otherwise player II wins. A winning strategy for a player wins against every play of the opponent, and the game is [determined](c:determinacy) when one of the players has one.
examples: For $A=\{x:x_0=0\}$, player I wins by playing $0$ first.
For $A=\{x:x_1=x_0\}$, player II wins by always choosing $x_1=x_0+1$.
For every Borel set $A$, the game $G(A)$ is determined, by the Borel determinacy theorem.
Non-example: rock-paper-scissors is not a Gale-Stewart game, because the players move at the same time, the play is finite, and the moves are not natural numbers chosen in turn.

reminder: A Galois connection between posets is a pair of monotone maps $f,g$ with $f(p)\le q$ exactly when $p\le g(q)$.
definition: A monotone Galois connection between [partially ordered sets](c:partial-order) $P$ and $Q$ is a pair of monotone maps $f:P\to Q$ and $g:Q\to P$ such that $f(p)\le q\iff p\le g(q)$ for all $p\in P$ and $q\in Q$. In the antitone version, $f$ and $g$ reverse the order and $q\le f(p)\iff p\le g(q)$.
examples: On $\mathbb R$, the inclusion $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ and the floor map satisfy $n\le x\iff n\le\lfloor x\rfloor$.
For a function $h:A\to B$, direct image and inverse image satisfy $h(S)\subseteq T\iff S\subseteq h^{-1}(T)$ for subsets $S\subseteq A$ and $T\subseteq B$.
For a finite Galois extension $L/K$, the correspondence between intermediate fields and subgroups of $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$ is an antitone Galois connection.
Non-example: on $\mathbb Z$, the monotone maps $f(n)=2n$ and $g(n)=n$ form no Galois connection, because $f(3)=6\not\le4$ while $3\le g(4)=4$.

steps: Regard a poset $P$ as a category with one morphism $p\to p'$ when $p\le p'$.
Then a monotone map is exactly a functor between two such categories.
The condition $f(p)\le q\iff p\le g(q)$ gives a bijection between $\mathrm{Hom}(f(p),q)$ and $\mathrm{Hom}(p,g(q))$, because both sets are empty or both have one element.
So $f$ is left adjoint to $g$, and the special case adds that each set of morphisms has at most one element.
links.why: Every fact on [adjoint functors](c:adjoint-functor), such as the preservation of colimits by left adjoints, holds for Galois connections.

reminder: A gauge field is the field of a gauge theory that mediates a force, described mathematically as a connection.
definition: In a gauge theory with [gauge group](c:gauge-group) $G$ on a spacetime $X$, a gauge field is a [connection](c:connection-on-a-bundle) on a principal $G$-bundle over $X$. Locally it is a 1-form $A$ with values in the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$, with field strength $F=dA+\tfrac12[A,A]$, and its quanta are the bosons that carry the force.
examples: The electromagnetic potential is a gauge field for $G=U(1)$, and $F$ is the electromagnetic field strength.
The gluon field of quantum chromodynamics is a gauge field for $G=SU(3)$.
The weak interaction and hypercharge form a gauge field for $SU(2)\times U(1)$, whose quanta mix into the $W^\pm$ bosons, the $Z$ boson and the photon.
Non-example: the electron field is a matter field, a section of a spinor bundle and not a connection, and its quanta are fermions.

steps: A [connection on a bundle](c:connection-on-a-bundle) tells how to compare the fibers over nearby points of the base.
In gauge theory the bundle is a principal $G$-bundle on spacetime, where $G$ is the gauge group.
A connection on it is a gauge field, and its curvature is the field strength $F$.
The special case adds the physical reading, in which the connection is a dynamical field and its quanta carry the force.
links.why: The geometry of connections and curvature describes gauge fields, and the physics adds the equations of motion.

reminder: The Gaussian integral of $e^{-ax^2}$ over the real line equals $\sqrt{\pi/a}$ for $a>0$.
definition: The Gaussian [integral](c:integral) is $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-ax^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi/a}$ for $a>0$, the integral of the [exponential function](c:exponential-function) of a negative quadratic. It extends to $\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-x^{\mathsf T}Ax}\,dx=\pi^{n/2}/\sqrt{\det A}$ for a positive definite symmetric matrix $A$ with [determinant](c:determinant) $\det A$, and to $\int e^{-ax^2+bx}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi/a}\,e^{b^2/(4a)}$.
examples: For $a=1/2$, the integral $\int e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi}$ is the normalizing constant of the standard normal density.
The integral $\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-|x|^2}\,dx$ equals $\pi^{n/2}$.
The half-line integral $\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx$ equals $\sqrt\pi/2$.
Non-example: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{x^2}\,dx$ diverges, because the exponent is positive.

reminder: A Gaussian process is a family of random variables in which every finite subfamily has a joint normal distribution.
definition: A Gaussian process indexed by a set $T$ is a family $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ of real [random variables](c:random-variable) such that, for all $t_1,\dots,t_n\in T$, the vector $(X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_n})$ has a multivariate [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution). Its law is determined by the mean $m(t)=\mathbb E X_t$, with [expected value](c:expected-value) $\mathbb E$, and by the covariance $k(s,t)=\operatorname{Cov}(X_s,X_t)$, which is a positive semidefinite kernel.
examples: Brownian motion is a Gaussian process with $m=0$ and $k(s,t)=\min(s,t)$.
The Brownian bridge on $[0,1]$ is a Gaussian process with $k(s,t)=\min(s,t)-st$.
A single Gaussian vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ is a Gaussian process indexed by $T=\{1,\dots,n\}$.
Non-example: the Poisson process is a stochastic process, but $N_t$ is Poisson distributed and not normal, so it is not Gaussian.

steps: A [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) is a family $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ of random variables on one probability space.
Require that every finite subfamily has a joint normal distribution.
Then all finite-dimensional distributions are determined by $m$ and $k$.
The special case adds the Gaussian condition, which makes the covariance function carry all the information.
links.why: A Gaussian process is described by two functions, a mean and a covariance, instead of a whole family of laws.

steps: [Brownian motion](c:brownian-motion) $(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ has $B_0=0$ and independent Gaussian increments, with $B_t-B_s$ of variance $t-s$.
A vector $(B_{t_1},\dots,B_{t_n})$ is a linear function of independent Gaussian increments.
A linear function of independent Gaussian variables is jointly Gaussian.
So Brownian motion is a Gaussian process with $m=0$ and $k(s,t)=\min(s,t)$.
links.why: Brownian motion is the basic Gaussian process, and the general concept allows other covariance functions.

reminder: The Gelfand spectrum of a commutative C*-algebra is the space of its characters, with the weak-* topology.
definition: For a [commutative C*-algebra](c:comm-c-star-algebra) $A$, the Gelfand spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is the set of characters, the nonzero algebra homomorphisms $\chi:A\to\mathbb C$ into the [complex numbers](c:complex-number), with the [weak-star topology](c:weak-star-topology). It is a [locally compact](c:locally-compact-space) Hausdorff space, and it is compact when $A$ has a unit. The Gelfand transform $a\mapsto(\chi\mapsto\chi(a))$ is an isometric $*$-isomorphism from $A$ onto the continuous functions on $\sigma(A)$ that vanish at infinity.
examples: For $A=C(X)$ with $X$ a compact Hausdorff space, we have $\sigma(A)\cong X$, where $x$ corresponds to evaluation at $x$.
For $A=\mathbb C^n$ with pointwise operations, the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is a discrete space with $n$ points.
For the unital C*-algebra generated by a normal operator $T$, the spectrum $\sigma(A)$ is the set of complex numbers that form the spectrum of $T$.
Non-example: the algebra $M_2(\mathbb C)$ is not commutative, and it has no nonzero character at all, because it is simple and has dimension $4$.
